# Svetra

This project's data layer is designed in `svetra.yaml`. Svetra checks it, compiles it into Postgres with row-level security on every table, TypeScript and Zod types, sign-in settings and access tests, and explains it in plain English. **You design with the person; Svetra makes it safe; you build the rest.**

Use the `svetra` MCP tools (`validate`, `compile`, `explain`, `context`, `graph`). If they aren't available, run the same commands with `npx -y svetra <command>`; add `--json` to `validate`.

## The loop

1. **Design first.** Turn the request into a change to `svetra.yaml`: entities, fields, policies, roles, `auth`, and holes only for logic that a policy can't express. Ask at most three questions, each with a recommended default, and only when the answer changes the design.
2. **Validate after every edit.** Fix every error using its `remediation.hint` before doing anything else. Never move on with errors. Warnings and info are worth reading: they usually point at a real gap.
3. **Plan a change** to an app that already exists (`svetra.yaml` is committed in git): call `plan` before compiling.
   - Tell the person every **destructive** line (data that would be deleted) and every **wider** line (people who'd see or change more), in their words.
   - Get their explicit yes in this conversation, then run `npx -y svetra plan --accept <kinds>`. Never accept on their behalf.
   - A rename is `was: <old name>` on the renamed entity or field, never a removal and an addition: that deletes every value.
4. **Compile.** Never edit what Svetra generates:
   - `supabase/schemas/svetra.sql`
   - `src/svetra.gen.ts`
   - `supabase/tests/svetra.test.sql`
   - the sign-in keys Svetra sets in `supabase/config.toml`

   Change `svetra.yaml` and compile again instead.
5. **Write only hole bodies,** in `supabase/holes/<name>.sql` (PL/pgSQL), **as statements only**: Svetra writes the `begin` and `end` around them, so never wrap the body in its own `begin … end`, and end every statement with `;`. A body that is a whole function makes `compile` refuse it (SVT032). Inputs are `p_<input>`, and `p_caller` is the signed-in person's id. A hole can touch only the entities in its `reads` and `writes`, and its `when` already decides who may call it, so don't repeat that check in the body. To let people join a team or start one, give the hole `grants: [<role>]` and insert into `"svetra"."role_grants"` in the body; never grant roles from app code.
6. **Explain.** Call `explain` and tell the person what changed in their words: who can see and change what, and "Before going live" when there is one. Never paste SQL at them.
7. **Prove it.** If a local Supabase is running, `supabase test db` runs the access tests as real users. Report failures exactly as they are.

## Rules

- **Never** use the service role key in app code, and never turn row-level security off.
- **Never** weaken a rule to make a test pass. A failing access test means the design and the database disagree; find out which is wrong.
- **Prefer a policy over a hole, and a hole over app code,** for anything about who can see or change data. A change of state on a row (draft to submitted, submitted to approved) is a policy with a `check`, not a hole: `when` is the row as it is, `check` is the row after, and `restrictive: true` narrows other rules.
- **App code calls holes** through the typed functions in `src/svetra.gen.ts`, such as `transfer(supabase, input)`.
- **Read the design with `context`**, not by opening the generated files.
- **When asked "who can see X?",** call `explain` again and answer from its lines, even if you called it earlier. Never answer from memory: the file may have changed since.

## The format, briefly

```yaml
svetra: "0.1"
system: Bookings
auth:
  sign_in: [email, google]
roles:
  admin: { description: "Runs the business", mfa: true }
  staff: { description: "Works at one location", scope: Location }
entities:
  Location:
    fields:
      id:   { type: uuid, primary: true }
      name: { type: text, required: true }
  Booking:
    fields:
      id:       { type: uuid, primary: true }
      customer: { type: user, required: true }
      location: { type: ref, entity: Location, required: true }
policies:
  customers_see_own:  { on: Booking, allow: [select, insert], when: "customer == auth.user" }
  staff_manage_local: { on: Booking, allow: [select, update], when: "has_role('staff', location)" }
  admins_run_locations: { on: Location, allow: [select, insert, update], when: "has_role('admin')" }
  staff_see_location: { on: Location, allow: [select], when: "has_role('staff', id)" }
holes:
  cancel:
    kind: function
    input: { booking: Booking.id }
    writes: [Booking]
    when: "booking.customer == auth.user"
```

The full specification is at https://github.com/555aaditya/Svetra/tree/main/docs.

1	# Rule: Commit granularity
2	
3	- When pushing work to GitHub (PRs, branches, any repo), **maximise the commit count**: break the work into the finest sensible steps and commit after each one, instead of one big commit.
4	- A step is one small logical change: one file or one tightly related set of edits that does one thing (a type and its first use, one test, one doc section, one fixture, one script). Typical PR: 6 to 20 commits, not 1 or 2.
5	- Each commit has a short imperative subject under 72 characters that says what that one step does. Keep the repo's own message conventions.
6	- Commit as you go, in the order the work was done and in a logical order (spec or doc first, then code, then tests, then fixtures and golden files, then changelog), so each commit reads on its own. Prefer commits that build and pass; where a step can't pass alone (a test before its code), say so in the subject or order them so the branch is green at the end.
7	- Never pad: no empty commits, no whitespace-only churn, no splitting a single line across commits to inflate the count. The goal is the most granular *real* history, not fake volume.
8	- Applies together with git-attribution.md (no credit lines in any commit) and the repo's own rules (for Svetra: one logical change per commit, small, imperative subject under 72 characters, signed identity as set in the repo's history).
9	- Work that is already pushed is not rewritten to follow this rule unless the user asks; apply it from the next push on.
10

# Rule: Commit granularity

- When pushing work to GitHub (PRs, branches, any repo), **maximise the commit count**: break the work into the finest sensible steps and commit after each one, instead of one big commit.
- A step is one small logical change: one file or one tightly related set of edits that does one thing (a type and its first use, one test, one doc section, one fixture, one script). Typical PR: 6 to 20 commits, not 1 or 2.
- Each commit has a short imperative subject under 72 characters that says what that one step does. Keep the repo's own message conventions.
- Commit as you go, in the order the work was done and in a logical order (spec or doc first, then code, then tests, then fixtures and golden files, then changelog), so each commit reads on its own. Prefer commits that build and pass; where a step can't pass alone (a test before its code), say so in the subject or order them so the branch is green at the end.
- Never pad: no empty commits, no whitespace-only churn, no splitting a single line across commits to inflate the count. The goal is the most granular *real* history, not fake volume.
- Applies together with git-attribution.md (no credit lines in any commit) and the repo's own rules (for Svetra: one logical change per commit, small, imperative subject under 72 characters, signed identity as set in the repo's history).
- Work that is already pushed is not rewritten to follow this rule unless the user asks; apply it from the next push on.

144	## 7. Alternatives considered
145	
146	- **Column privileges** (`grant update (status) on doc to authenticated`). They are per database role, not per row or state, so they can't say "only while the document is submitted", and the approvals rule needs exactly that. They are the lighter tool for a field **nobody** may change after creation, such as `author` or `created_at`. That is a different, simpler feature, a field flag `immutable: true` (Open **C6**), and it could share the same tests.
147	- **A `check` constraint.** It sees one row, so it can't compare old and new.

`SVT036` is the column-rule twin of `SVT034`: a combination of policies that does something neither says alone. The hint is to give the freeing policy an `only` too, or to merge the two.

## 7. Alternatives considered

- **Column privileges** (`grant update (status) on doc to authenticated`). They are per database role, not per row or state, so they can't say "only while the document is submitted", and the approvals rule needs exactly that. They are the lighter tool for a field **nobody** may change after creation, such as `author` or `created_at`. That is a different, simpler feature, a field flag `immutable: true` (Open **C6**), and it could share the same tests.
- **A `check` constraint.** It sees one row, so it can't compare old and new.
- **A view with `instead of` triggers.** Heavier, and the API would have to be pointed at the view.
- **A list of fields that can't change (`unchanged`)** is the same power, written the other way round, and the first draft of this document used it. It fails open: a column added later is free for everyone the rule was meant to limit. The approvals prompt itself is an allow-list ("cannot change anything else"). Open **C1**.
- **Leave it to holes and hand-written triggers.** This is what happens today, and what the agent evaluation measured: four of four agents wrote the trigger by hand, outside the design, where it isn't explained, tested or diffed. A rule Svetra can't see is a rule Svetra can't prove.
- **Check it in the app.** Not enforceable: the browser talks to the database directly.

## 8. The approvals app, complete

```yaml
  reviewers_decide:
    on: Doc
    allow: [update]
    when:  "reviewer == auth.user and status == 'submitted'"
    check: "reviewer == auth.user and status in ['approved', 'rejected']"
    only: [status]
```

With this single added line, the whole prompt is in `svetra.yaml`: the author's rules, the reviewer's, the transitions, and the column rule. No hole, no hand-written SQL, and every one of the 24 oracle checks is expected to pass, including "the reviewer cannot approve and retitle at once". Add a `notes` column to `Doc` next month and the reviewer still can't edit it, with no change to the rule.

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/555aaditya/Svetra/main/schema/svetra.schema.json
svetra: "0.1"
system: Approvals

auth:
  sign_in: [email]

entities:
  Doc:

policies:
  authors_see_own:
    on: Doc
    allow: [select]
    when: "author == auth.user"

  reviewers_see_submitted:
    on: Doc
    allow: [select]
    when: "reviewer == auth.user and status != 'draft'"

  authors_create_drafts:
    on: Doc
    allow: [insert]
    check: "author == auth.user and status == 'draft' and reviewer != auth.user"

  authors_edit_drafts:
    on: Doc
    allow: [update]
    when: "author == auth.user and status == 'draft'"
    check: "author == auth.user and status in ['draft', 'submitted']"
    only: [title, status]

  authors_delete_drafts:
    on: Doc
    allow: [delete]
    when: "author == auth.user and status == 'draft'"

  reviewers_decide:
    on: Doc
    allow: [update]
    when: "reviewer == auth.user and author != auth.user and status == 'submitted'"
    check: "reviewer == auth.user and status in ['approved', 'rejected']"
    only: [status]

{"text":"Approvals

What your app stores
  Docs
    - the signed-in person who owns it (required)
    - reviewer: a signed-in person (required)
    - title: text (required)
    - status: one of draft, submitted, approved or rejected (required) (starts as draft)

Signing in
  - People sign in with email (a password or an emailed link).
  - Anyone can create an account.
  - People confirm their email address before they can sign in.
  - Passwords need at least 10 characters.

Who can see and change what
  Docs
    - Signed-in people can see a doc when its author is them.
    - Signed-in people can see a doc when its reviewer is them and its status is not draft.
    - Signed-in people can create a doc when its author is them and its status is draft and its reviewer is not them.

    - Signed-in people can change a doc when its reviewer is them and its author is not them and its status is submitted. After the change, its reviewer is them and its status is approved or rejected. They can change only its status.
    - Nobody can see docs any other way.

Before going live
  - Set up your own email sender (SMTP). Supabase's built-in sender is for testing and only sends a few emails an hour.
  - Set your app's real web address in Supabase, for sign-in links and the page people return to after signing in.
"}

**What the database allows**
- **Seeing:** the author always sees their own documents. The reviewer sees a document only once it is submitted. Nobody else sees any.

- **Approved or rejected:** no rule allows any change or delete, so the document is frozen.

The rule that "the reviewer can't change anything but the status" is enforced by a generated trigger on update, not by the row policies alone. I added no custom code or holes.
